newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Bull run in Russia, East Europe may slow.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Bull run in Russia, East Europe may slow.

text.p: More players, more issues but lower returns are expected for the fixed income markets in Russia and East Europe in 1997, U.S. experts said.
Investors expect 1997 to be less bountiful than 1996, which so far has seen Russia debt double in value while Poland has risen 35 percent and Bulgaria 28 percent, they said.

This year's heady ride, of course, followed the 1995 liquidity crunch brought by rising U.S. interest rates, while next year's performance will be compared to the much stronger baseline levels of 1996.

Analysts were less optimistic about 1997 growth than the Russian government official forecast of two percent. However, Peter Allen, head of emerging markets research at Bank of Boston, insisted "there's still some upside" for investors in Eastern Europe.

Russia's return to the Eurobond market has raised hopes that more sovereign, municipal and corporate debt would follow. Poland and Hungary are also prime candidates for issuing Eurobonds this year, analysts said.
As for Russia, "Future Eurobond issues can do better than 345 basis points," Allen said, referring to the pricing of Russia's inaugural $1 billion 3-year global bond in November.

Considering Russia as a "solid double-B" credit, he expected the yield of the principal of Russia's "when-issued" restructured loans to drop by 200 to 300 basis points from its current spread of over 700 basis points. Russia received a sovereign credit rating of BB-minus from Standard and Poor's and Ba2 from Moody's.

Vladimir Kvint, senior consultant at Arthur Andersen Economic Consulting, said Russia's political risk has diminished with a succession of free parliamentary and presidential elections, and portfolio investments have risen to reflect the changing perception.

Kvint estimated that foreign direct investment would touch $3 billion this year, up from $2 billion in 1995. Yet he said he thinks foreign investment remains paltry if one considers Russia's wealth of natural resources, educated labor force and well-developed industrial infrastructure.
What is holding foreign investors back from directly participating in Russia's epochal transformation?
Long-term foreign investors still fear Russia's financial instability, Kvint asserted.

He said a financial crisis could erupt in five months, noting that Russian citizens have been putting $2 billion to $3 billion worth of roubles per month into foreign currencies. Their savings -- estimated at 25 percent of the gross domestic product -- are not deployed productively in the Russian economy, he added.
Kvint did not expect Russia's economic growth to turn positive as Russian officials have projected. Instead, he expected a contraction of one percent in 1997.

Faced with mounting wage arrears and social unrest, the central bank may not resist the temptation to print roubles, leading to rising inflation and currency devaluation, he said. The specter of devaluation could speed capital flight from Russia and reverse the portfolio investment flow, he said.
This could prompt investment in East Europe to spread between large markets of Poland and the Czech republic and smaller new markets of Slovenia and Romania, he added.

But Jaroslaw Aranowicz, senior European analyst at Freimark, Blair and Co., doubted a financial crisis would happen in Russia. He pointed to the economy's resilience and promising progress on tax collection by the government.
But he agreed with Kvint's assessment that under-investment would limit Russia's economic growth, predicting a flat growth rate for 1997, compared to the official forecast of a two-percent rise.
Among East European markets, Poland is poised to shine as a result of strong economic growth, a low budget deficit and progress in privatization, he said.

After leaping into the investment-grade league and launching its $500 million global bond this year, Poland is expected to issue $1 billion in Eurobonds to retire the expensive discount Brady bonds. Polish banks may also begin tapping the Eurobond market, Aranowicz said.

Another candidate for Eurobond issues would be Hungary, which, with its BB-plus/Ba1 rating, could raise 10-year debt at 80 basis points over comparable U.S. Treasuries, or 20-year debt at 130 basis points over, he estimated.
Bulgaria is expected to remain the ultimate high-yielder, lurching from crisis to crisis, Aranowitz predicted.
By adopting the currency board, the socialist government would have access to International Monetary Fund assistance.
This would allow them to avert default on the $300 million debt payment, due in January, he said.
But for the implementation of the currency board, which requires an overhaul of the economic system, Bulgaria's Socialist government may lack both the will and the capability, Aranowicz said.
